opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it goes back to something very basic about the world we live in. The world has objects in it, and those objects have properties and stand in relations to one another. If you want a system to know things about that world, you need a language that can talk about objects and relations in a general way: "every person has a mother," "if two blocks are stacked, the bottom one can't be moved." Those are statements that hold across an unbounded number of cases.

If your representation lacks that expressive power, if it's essentially propositional, like a Boolean circuit or, to a large extent, a standard neural network, then you can't state those rules once. You have to effectively write them out separately for every instance. Take the rules of chess. In first-order logic they fit on a page or two. In a propositional language they run to something like a million pages, because you have to say the same thing over and over for every square, every piece, every time step. That isn't just an aesthetic problem. It means the system needs vastly more data to learn the same regularity, because it has to learn every instance separately rather than learning the general rule.

I think that's a big part of why we see today's large models, impressive as they are, consume enormous amounts of data and still make strange errors. They seem to learn large collections of fragments of the regularity rather than the regularity itself. Go programs that play at superhuman level can be defeated by fairly simple adversarial strategies, which suggests they never really grasped the concept of a connected group of stones the way a human player does.

What we tried to do with probabilistic programming languages, BLOG and others, was to combine that expressiveness with the ability to handle uncertainty. Historically, AI had logic, which was expressive but couldn't deal with uncertainty, and probability, which handled uncertainty but was essentially propositional. Bayesian networks are wonderful, but they are fundamentally propositional. Bringing the two together gives you a representation that can describe a world with unknown objects, uncertain identity, uncertain relations, and still reason about it coherently.

We used that, for example, in monitoring for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty: detecting seismic events from a global network of sensors. You don't know how many events there are or which signals come from which event. An expressive probabilistic model could state the physics of the problem compactly and then do the inference, and it performed substantially better than the system that had been in use.

So for me, expressive power isn't a luxury. It's what lets you capture knowledge compactly, learn it from reasonable amounts of data, and generalize correctly to situations you've never seen. I don't think we'll get robust, trustworthy general intelligence without it, however much we scale up the circuits.

r001.rationale: The response calls Bayesian networks fundamentally propositional, but does not describe them as a probabilistic generalization of Boolean circuits.

r002.rationale: It says a representation must express objects and relations and encode general rules compactly, explaining that propositional forms require unwieldy instance-by-instance expansions.

r003.rationale: The response criticizes propositional representations and discusses circuit-like systems, but does not reject giant circuits as a plausible account of how people represent knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a very simple observation: the world is made of objects, and those objects have relations to each other. There are people, there are cities, there are molecules, there are chess pieces, and the facts we care about are facts about how those things relate. If your representation can't say "every person has a mother" without enumerating every person, or can't express "the king is in check if some opposing piece attacks the square it's on" without spelling out all the board positions, then you're in trouble. You end up with a representation that's exponentially larger than the knowledge it's trying to capture.

That's really the lesson that logic taught us in the twentieth century. First-order logic is powerful precisely because it lets you quantify over objects and state general rules, and those rules then apply to situations you've never encountered. A propositional system, or a system that's essentially a big lookup table, doesn't have that. You can train it on a billion examples and it still doesn't know the rule, it just knows the examples.

And the same thing happened with probability. Bayesian networks were a huge advance, but they're propositional. If you want to reason about an unknown number of objects, about whether two records refer to the same person or whether there's an undetected aircraft out there, you need a formalism that combines the expressive power of first-order logic with the ability to handle uncertainty. That's why I've spent so much time on probabilistic programming and open-universe models, because that combination is what you need to describe the real world, where you don't know in advance what exists.

Now, the deep learning community has sometimes argued that expressiveness doesn't matter, that you can just learn everything end to end from data. And the systems are remarkable, I don't dispute that. But I think what we're seeing is that these systems struggle exactly where expressiveness matters: on compositional generalization, on reasoning about novel combinations of known facts, on anything that requires a general rule to be applied reliably in a new context. They've learned a vast number of specific patterns, but the patterns don't compose the way a quantified statement composes.

So my view is that expressive power isn't a philosophical luxury. It's about data efficiency and generalization. A system with the right expressive power can learn from one example what a less expressive system needs a million examples to approximate, and it can be confident about cases it has never seen, because it actually represents the structure of the world rather than a statistical shadow of it. Ultimately, if we want systems that are reliable, that can explain themselves, and that humans can actually trust, I think they'll need representations that are rich enough to say what's true.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls Bayesian networks a propositional advance, but does not characterize them as probabilistic generalizations of Boolean circuits.

r002.rationale: It says representations should express general rules without enumerating every case, which avoids becoming exponentially larger than the knowledge they capture.

r003.rationale: The candidate criticizes lookup-table representations, but does not reject giant circuits implementing appropriate functions as an account of how people represent knowledge.

astra-6.text:
Well, the world has far more structure than you can capture with a fixed list of features. We talk about objects, relationships, events, and general rules. You can say, for example, that every person has a mother without having to list every person and their mother. An expressive representation lets you state that general fact compactly and apply it to individuals you’ve never encountered before.

And we need to represent uncertainty about those things, too. We may not know which objects exist, how they’re related, or what caused an event. So we want languages that combine the ability to describe a richly structured world with the ability to express uncertainty.

The challenge, of course, is that being able to express something doesn’t mean you can reason about it efficiently. But if your language can’t express the relevant knowledge at all, then no amount of computation is going to make up for that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expressive representations and uncertainty but does not characterize Bayesian networks or Boolean circuits.

r002.rationale: It says a representation must describe the relevant structured knowledge and gives a general fact that can be stated compactly rather than listed for every individual.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss giant circuits or reject them as an account of how people represent knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, expressive power determines what you can say, and therefore what you can learn and reason about. If your representation can only describe a fixed collection of attributes, then you're going to have difficulty expressing things like, “Every person has a mother.” You can record a mother for each individual you've encountered, but that's different from stating a general fact that applies to individuals you've never encountered.

This was one of the great advantages of first-order logic: you could talk about objects, relations among objects, and general rules, without listing every possible instance. A compact statement could cover an enormous number of situations.

Of course, expressiveness comes with computational costs. You don't get efficient reasoning for free just by choosing a richer language. But if the language can't express the structure of the world, then making the inference algorithm faster isn't going to solve the problem. We need representations rich enough to capture that structure, including uncertainty, and then methods that let us reason with them effectively.

r001.rationale: The response discusses first-order logic and richer representations, but does not characterize Bayesian networks as probabilistic generalizations of Boolean circuits.

r002.rationale: It says representations must be rich enough to capture the world's structure and gives a compact general statement as an alternative to listing every instance, conveying that needed knowledge should be expressible in manageable form.

r003.rationale: It does not reject giant circuits as a plausible account of how people represent knowledge.
